# The Mathematics of Portfolio Return (continued)

## ANNUALISED RETURNS {#a}

When comparing returns over long periods it is easier to think in terms of standardised periods, annual returns being the most convenient. The average (or mean) annual return over a number of years can be calculated arithmetically or geometrically as follows:

**Arithmetic average or average return**

$$\bar{r}_A = \frac{f}{n} \times \sum_{i=1}^{i=n} r_i \tag{3.31}$$

**Geometric average or annualised return**

$$\widetilde{r} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1 + r_i)\right)^{\frac{f}{n}} - 1 \tag{3.32}$$

where: $n$ = the number of periods under analysis

$f$ = the number of periods within the year (monthly $f = 12$, quarterly $f = 4$)

The geometric average or annualised return is the return which, if compounded with itself for the cumulative period, will result in the cumulative return.

Average and annualised returns are calculated in Exhibit 3.23.

> **⚠ Caution**
>
> It is poor performance practice to annualise returns for short periods (less than one year). It is inappropriate to assume the rate of return achieved in the year to date will continue for the remainder of the year.

> **Note**
>
> The terms "arithmetic" and "geometric" are common in the field of performance measurement; arithmetic reflects additive relationships and geometric reflects multiplicative or compounding relationships.

### Exhibit 3.23 — Average and annualised returns {#b}

**Annual returns**

| Year | Return |
| --- | --- |
| 2003 | 10.5% |
| 2002 | −5.6% |
| 2001 | 23.4% |
| 2000 | −15.7% |
| 1999 | 8.9% |

Cumulative return:

$$(1.105 \times 0.944 \times 1.234 \times 0.843 \times 1.089) - 1 = 18.2\%$$

Arithmetic average:

$$\frac{10.5\% - 5.6\% + 23.4\% - 15.7\% + 8.9\%}{5} = 4.3\%$$

If the annual average return is compounded for five years the cumulative return is considerably greater than 18.2%:

$$(1.043 \times 1.043 \times 1.043 \times 1.043 \times 1.043) - 1 = 23.4\%$$

Geometric average or annualised return:

$$(1.105 \times 0.944 \times 1.234 \times 0.843 \times 1.089)^{\frac{1}{5}} - 1 = 3.4\%$$

As expected, if the annualised return is compounded for five years the cumulative return remains the same:

$$(1.034 \times 1.034 \times 1.034 \times 1.034 \times 1.034) - 1 = 18.2\%$$

---

Investment returns compound. When assessing historic performance, it is essential to use the constant rate of return that will compound to the same value as the historic series of returns, as shown in Exhibit 3.24.

### Exhibit 3.24 — Positive bias {#c}

Assume the rate of return is +20% in the first period and −20% in the second period

Assuming a start value of £100

The value at the end of the first period is £120

The value at the end of the second period is £96

The arithmetic average is

$$\frac{20.0\% - 20.0\%}{2} = 0\%$$

The annualised return is

$$(1.2 \times 0.8)^{\frac{1}{2}} - 1 = -2.02\%$$

−2.02% compounded over the two periods will generate the accurate end value of £96.

> **Note**
>
> Arithmetic averages are positively biased; if returns are not constant the annualised return will always be less than the arithmetic average. Note that the annualised return when compounded with itself over the entire period will reconcile to the original cumulative return, whereas the arithmetic average return will not. Hence the annualised return provides a better indicator of wealth at the end of the period than the arithmetic average. Performance analysts should use annualised rather than average returns.

The average return is always greater than or equal to the annualised return:

$$\bar{r}_A \geq \widetilde{r} \tag{3.33}$$

A good approximation of the difference can be calculated from:

$$\widetilde{r} \cong \bar{r}_A - \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \tag{3.34}$$

where: $\sigma$ = the standard deviation or variability of returns<sup>23</sup>

This is an important relationship; the amount by which the annualised return is less than the average return depends on variability. The greater the variability of returns, the greater the difference between the arithmetic average and the geometric average.

If the average return is 12.0% and the variability of returns is 10% then the annualised return is approximately $12.0\% - (10.0\%)^2 / 2 = 11.5\%$.

### Since-inception internal rate of return (SI-IRR) {#d}

To calculate the "annual" internal rate of return rather than the "cumulative" rate of return for the entire period we need to solve for $r$ using the following formula:

$$V_E = V_S \times (1 + r)^Y + \sum_{t=1}^{t=T} C_t \times (1 + r)^{W_t^y} \tag{3.35}$$

where:

$Y$ = length of time period to be measured in years

$W_t^y$ = factor to be applied to external cash flow on day $t$

$$W_t^y = Y - Y_t \tag{3.36}$$

where: $Y_t$ = number of years since the beginning of the period of measurement

For example, assume cash flow occurs on the 236th day of the third year for a total measurement period of five years; then:

$$W_t^y = 5 - 2\frac{236}{365} = 2\frac{129}{365}$$

For presentational purposes, internal rates of return are often calculated since inception and annualised.

### Modified IRR (MIRR) {#e}

The modified IRR or MIRR is an ex-ante IRR approach that addresses two of the criticisms of the ex-ante IRR: the reinvestment of future cash flows at the IRR rate and the potential for multiple correct solutions. The modified IRR assumes that positive cash flows are reinvested at an assumed reinvestment rate and negative cash flows are financed at an assumed cost of capital. Clearly the reinvestment rate and cost of capital are of more concern for project appraisal than the measurement of asset performance. The MIRR is the ratio of the sum of assumed end value equivalent of positive cash flows (including the end value) divided by the present value of negative cash flows including the start value:

$$MIRR = \sqrt[n]{\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{t=t} V_E + C_t^+ \times (1 + rr)^{W_t^y}}{\sum_{t=1}^{t=T} V_S + C_t^- \times (1 + coc)^{-W_t^y}}} - 1 \tag{3.37}$$

where:

$coc$ = cost of capital

$rr$ = reinvestment rate

$C_t^+$ = positive cash flow on day $t$

$C_t^-$ = negative cash flow on day $t$

Performance analysts, focusing on ex-post analysis, are unlikely to use an ex-ante statistic using assumed reinvestment rates such as MIRR but for completeness an example calculation is shown in Exhibit 3.25.

### Exhibit 3.25 — Modified IRR {#f}

| Initial outlay | Cash flow Year 1 | Cash flow Year 2 | Cash flow Year 3 | Cash flow Year 4 | Final value Year 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| £150m | £50m | £22m | £35m | −£45m | £330m |

Assume a cost of capital of 8% and a reinvestment rate of 5%.

Final cash equivalent of outflows:

$$330 + 45 \times (1.05) = 377.25$$

Present value of inflows:

$$150 + \frac{50}{1.08} + \frac{22}{(1.08)^2} + \frac{35}{(1.08)^3} = 242.94$$

$$MIRR = \sqrt[5]{\frac{377.25}{242.94}} - 1 = 9.2\%$$

> **Note**
>
> Excel® offers a modified IRR function, MIRR.

### Return hiatus {#g}

If there is any hiatus or gap in the performance track record, however short, it is impossible to bridge the gap and link performance returns to produce cumulative and hence annualised returns.

> **⚠ Caution**
>
> Some performance analysts might argue that it is possible to substitute an index return for a gap in performance and therefore calculate cumulative and annualised return. This is clearly not good practice and should be avoided.
